title: Lab-Grown Diamonds
passage:
Diamonds have long been valued for their rarity. Today, however, scientists can produce diamonds in laboratories that are [1] natural ones. They have the same chemical structure and hardness, and even experts need special equipment to tell them apart.

Lab-grown diamonds are usually much cheaper than mined diamonds, and their popularity has grown rapidly, especially among younger buyers. Many of these consumers say they prefer lab-grown stones because mining can damage the environment and has sometimes been linked to poor working conditions. [2], the traditional diamond industry argues that natural diamonds have a unique history that makes them more meaningful as gifts.

The rise of lab-grown diamonds has caused the prices of both types to fall. Some analysts believe that, in the future, diamonds may [3], becoming affordable accessories rather than rare luxury items.

title: School Uniforms
passage:
In many countries, debates about school uniforms continue. Supporters argue that uniforms [1]. When all students wear the same clothes, differences in family income are less visible, which may reduce bullying and peer pressure to buy expensive brands.

Opponents, however, say that uniforms limit students' freedom of expression. They also point out that uniforms are not always cheap. [2], families often have to buy several sets, as well as special shoes and bags, which can be costly for parents with more than one child.

Research on the effects of uniforms has produced mixed results. Some studies have found small improvements in attendance and behavior, while others found no clear difference. As a result, some schools have adopted a compromise, such as [3], allowing students to choose from a limited range of clothing in certain colors.

多くの国で、制服をめぐる議論が続いている。支持する人たちは、制服は生徒の間の平等を促すと主張する。全員が同じ服を着れば家庭の収入の差が見えにくくなり、いじめや、高価なブランドを買わなければという同調圧力が減るかもしれない。

しかし反対する人たちは、制服は生徒の自己表現の自由を制限すると言う。また、制服は必ずしも安くないとも指摘する。実際、家庭は何着も買わなければならないことが多く、専用の靴やかばんも必要なので、子どもが複数いる親には負担が大きい。

title: Citizen Science
passage:
Scientists are increasingly asking members of the public to help with research. In so-called citizen science projects, volunteers collect data such as bird sightings, weather measurements, or photographs of stars. Because thousands of people can take part, these projects can [1] that professional researchers could never gather on their own.

For example, an annual bird count in North America involves tens of thousands of volunteers. The data they collect has helped scientists understand how climate change is affecting bird migration. [2], online projects allow volunteers to classify galaxies or identify animals in camera-trap photos from their own homes.

Some scientists have worried about the quality of data collected by amateurs. However, studies have shown that, with clear instructions and checks, volunteer data can be [3]. In addition, many participants say the projects have increased their interest in science and nature.

title: Fast Fashion
passage:
Fast fashion refers to clothing that is designed, produced, and sold quickly and cheaply to follow the latest trends. While it has made fashionable clothes [1], it has also created serious environmental problems. The textile industry uses enormous amounts of water and is responsible for a significant share of global carbon emissions.

Another problem is waste. Because cheap clothes are often worn only a few times, millions of tons of clothing are thrown away every year. [2], only a small percentage of discarded clothing is recycled into new garments, as many fabrics are made from blends of materials that are difficult to separate.

Some brands have responded by offering repair services or collecting used clothes in their stores. Critics argue, however, that these efforts will have little impact unless companies [3]. They believe the real solution is for consumers to buy fewer, higher-quality items and keep them for longer.

title: Sleep and Teenagers

The results have been encouraging. In one study, when a high school moved its start time from 7:50 to 8:45 a.m., students slept longer, their attendance improved, and their grades rose slightly. However, changing school hours is not always easy, as it can [3], such as bus schedules, after-school sports, and parents' work hours.

title: Tiny Houses
passage:
In recent years, some people have chosen to live in "tiny houses," homes that are usually smaller than 40 square meters. For many owners, the main reason is cost. Tiny houses are [1], allowing owners to avoid large mortgages and spend more money on travel or hobbies.

Others are attracted by the idea of a simpler lifestyle. Living in a small space forces people to own fewer possessions, which many say reduces stress. Tiny houses also use less energy for heating and cooling. [2], some people find that living in such a small space is more difficult than they expected, especially for families with children.

Another challenge is finding a place to build. In many areas, local regulations set minimum sizes for houses, making it illegal to live in a tiny house permanently. Some cities have begun to [3], hoping that tiny houses can help address the shortage of affordable housing.

title: The Value of Boredom

Those who had done the boring task came up with more ideas than a group that had not. [2], researchers suggest that boredom encourages the mind to wander, which can lead to new ideas.

This does not mean that people should try to be bored all the time. Psychologists say, however, that allowing ourselves short periods without entertainment — for example, during a walk or a train ride — may [3].

title: Food Waste Apps
passage:
Every day, restaurants, bakeries, and supermarkets throw away large amounts of food that is still safe to eat. To tackle this problem, several smartphone apps now allow businesses to [1]. Users can buy a bag of unsold bread or prepared meals for a fraction of the original price and pick it up just before closing time.

The apps have become popular with both businesses and customers. Shops can recover some of their costs and reduce the amount of waste they produce, while customers enjoy cheap meals. [2], because users often do not know exactly what their bag will contain, the apps add an element of surprise that many people enjoy.

However, some experts point out that these apps deal with the symptoms rather than the cause. They argue that to truly reduce food waste, businesses need to [3], for example by using better data to predict demand.
